summary: Describes how to carry structured NxDS0 TDM signals, as used in telephone networks, over packet networks as pseudowires. It is the structure-aware companion to RFC 4553. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Old telephone circuits put each call in a numbered slot in a repeating frame. This memo describes how to carry those frames across an IP network in packets while keeping the slot structure intact, so the receiving end can rebuild a real telephone circuit rather than just a stream of bits.

subtitle: Carrying structured telephone circuits over a packet network without losing the time-slot structure.

tldr.problem: Telephone networks carry voice on fixed time slots, and the standard way to move those circuits over an IP network treats the bit stream as an opaque blob, so the structure is lost.
tldr.mechanism: CESoPSN defines an encapsulation for structured NxDS0 circuits. Each packet carries a fixed number of time slots from a set of frames, a 4-byte control word says what state the circuit is in, and an optional fixed RTP header carries timing, while a jitter buffer at the far end absorbs the variation in packet delay.
tldr.outcome: The document is an Informational specification of the encapsulation. It fits the PWE3 pseudowire architecture, and it is the structure-aware companion to the structure-agnostic work in RFC 4553.

today: RFC 5086 is an Informational document published in December 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies the encapsulation layer only, leaving the pseudowire setup and the control protocol to other documents, and it is the structure-aware companion to RFC 4553.

sections.title: What CESoPSN Does
sections.content:
CESoPSN describes a method for encapsulating structured NxDS0 Time Division Multiplexed signals as pseudowires over packet-switching networks. It complements the work on structure-agnostic emulation of TDM bit streams in RFC 4553: where that work treats the TDM signal as a stream of bits with no structure, CESoPSN knows where the frames and time slots begin and carries that structure across the network.

Emulating NxDS0 circuits saves packet network bandwidth and supports grooming at the level of individual DS0 channels and distributed cross-connect. It also makes the customer equipment more resilient to the effects of lost packets, because a lost packet can be replaced by an equivalent amount of replacement data.

The solution fits the Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge architecture in RFC 3985, satisfies the general requirements of RFC 3916, and meets the specific requirements for structured TDM emulation in RFC 4197. The TDM payload is encapsulated without any changes, following the principle of minimum intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to move a telephone circuit over IP. One treats it as a raw bit stream and does not know what the bits mean. The other knows where each frame and time slot starts, and that is what this memo specifies, so the receiving end can rebuild a real circuit.

sections.title: Terminology and Design Constraints
sections.content:
The document uses the terms from the PWE3 and structured TDM emulation documents, plus the vocabulary of telephone networks. Loss of Signal is the condition where a valid TDM signal cannot be extracted from the physical layer of the trunk. The Frame Alignment Signal is a periodic pattern that imposes the TDM structure on E1 and T1 circuits, and Out of Frame Synchronization is the state of the receiver when it fails to find a valid frame alignment signal; handling that condition includes invalidation of the TDM data. An Alarm Indication Signal is a bit pattern in the TDM stream indicating an upstream circuit outage. The Remote Alarm Indication and Remote Defect Indication are patterns in the framing sent back by the receiver that experiences an alarm, and cannot be detected while loss of signal, out of frame synchronization or an alarm is present. The Interworking Function is the functional block that segments and encapsulates TDM into CESoPSN packets and, in the reverse direction, decapsulates them and reconstitutes the TDM.

The protocol was designed around four constraints. First, all the packets belonging to a given pseudowire must carry the same amount of TDM data, which simplifies replacing a lost packet with one carrying exactly the same amount of replacement data. Second, implementations should provide the same end-to-end delay between a given pair of customer edges regardless of the bit rate of the emulated service. Third, implementations should support packetization latencies in the range 1 to 5 milliseconds, and those that allow the latency to be configured must do so with a granularity that is a multiple of 125 microseconds. Fourth, there is a common data path for services with and without customer edge application signaling: where signaling must also be transferred for the normal operation of the emulated service, it is passed in dedicated signaling packets, while the format and processing of the packets carrying TDM data stay unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo borrows the telephone vocabulary for faults, and then sets four rules the design has to obey. The important one is that every packet carries the same amount of voice data, so a lost packet can be replaced exactly.

sections.title: The Encapsulation and the Control Word
sections.content:
The CESoPSN header must contain the CESoPSN control word, 4 bytes long, and may also contain a fixed RTP header. When the RTP header is included it must follow the control word, except with UDP demultiplexing, where it must precede it, so that the header compression mechanisms for IPv4 and IPv6 with UDP work, the PWE3 control word sits right after the MPLS label to keep pseudowires safe for equal-cost multipath, and the same packet format can be used for both MPLS and L2TPv3 segments so they can be stitched together. The total size of a CESoPSN packet for a pseudowire must not exceed the path MTU between the two ends. With an IPv4 packet network, the Don't Fragment flag must be set. The destination UDP port is used to multiplex and demultiplex individual pseudowires and acts as the pseudowire label, so the ports must be configured by hand at both ends, and the configured destination port together with the source and destination IP addresses identifies the pseudowire for the receiver. Ports used as pseudowire labels should fall in the dynamically allocated range, 49152 through 65535, and because port-translating middleboxes make traversal harder, it is not recommended to use UDP-based pseudowires where such middleboxes sit between the ends.

The control word has the same structure for every combination of packet network and multiplexing mechanism. Bits 0 to 3 follow the PWE3 control word and must be zero unless they indicate the start of an Associated Channel Header, which is needed if the state of the pseudowire is monitored using Virtual Circuit Connectivity Verification. The L bit indicates an abnormal condition of the attachment circuit. The M field is a 2-bit modifier that, when L is clear, discriminates signaling packets and carries the remote defect indication across the network; when L is set, only the value 00 is defined. The R bit is set by the network-bound interworking function to say that its local customer-edge-bound counterpart has lost a pre-configured number of consecutive packets, and must be cleared once that counterpart has received a pre-configured number of consecutive packets. The FRG bits must be cleared for all services except trunk-specific NxDS0 with channel-associated signaling, where they may denote fragmentation of the multiframe structures. The LEN field may carry the length of the CESoPSN packet, defined as the header plus the payload, when it is less than 64 bytes, and must be zero otherwise. The sequence number provides the common pseudowire sequencing function and the detection of lost packets; its space is a 16-bit unsigned circular space, its initial value should be random and unpredictable, and it must be incremented with each data packet sent on the pseudowire.

The L and M bits together form a 3-bit code point space with eight values. Code point 0 with L clear is a data packet in a normal situation, whose payload must be played out as received. With L clear and M set to 10, the packet carries the remote defect indication condition of the attachment circuit. With L set and M set to 00, the TDM data is invalid and the payload may be omitted, and implementations must insert the configured idle code in the outgoing attachment circuit. The remaining code points are reserved for future extensions or for CESoPSN signaling packets, and implementations that do not support the reserved code points must silently discard the corresponding packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet has a small 4-byte header saying what state the circuit is in, plus the voice data. The header has a bit for faults on the near end, a bit that says the far end has lost packets, a two-bit modifier, a length field and a sequence number so lost packets can be spotted.

sections.title: The Payload and the Packetization Latencies
sections.content:
The payload of a CESoPSN packet always consists of a fixed number of octets filled, octet by octet, with the data contained in the corresponding basic structures. The order of the payload octets corresponds to their order on the TDM attachment circuit, and consecutive bits fill each octet from its most significant bit to its least significant one. All packets must carry the same amount of valid TDM data in both directions, so the time taken to fill a packet is constant, and the two ends must agree the number of payload octets when the pseudowire is set up. A packet may omit invalid TDM data to save bandwidth, in which case the L bit must be set.

For the basic NxDS0 service, the structure preserved across the packet network consists of N octets filled with the data of the corresponding NxDS0 channels belonging to the same frame of the originating trunks, and the service generates 8000 such structures per second. The basic structures must be aligned with the packet payload boundaries, so the amount of TDM data in a packet must be an integer multiple of the basic structure size and the first structure must start immediately at the beginning of the payload. Packetization latency, number of timeslots and payload size are linked by L = 8 * N * D, where D is the packetization latency in milliseconds, L is the packet payload size in octets and N is the number of DS0 channels.

Implementations supporting NxDS0 services must support a fixed set of configurable packetization latencies. For N = 1 the latency is 8 milliseconds with a packet payload size of 64 bytes. For 2 <= N <= 4 it is 4 milliseconds with a payload size of 32 * N bytes. For N >= 5 it is 1 millisecond with a payload size of 8 * N octets. Support for the 5 millisecond latency when N = 1 is recommended, and any other latency compatible with the restrictions is optional.

The document defines a single format for packets carrying TDM data regardless of whether channel-associated signaling or other customer edge application signaling has to be carried, and that basic service can be extended to carry such signaling in separate signaling packets, which may travel in the same pseudowire or in a separate dedicated one. It also defines dedicated formats for NxDS0 services with channel-associated signaling in signaling sub-structures inside some packets, which differ according to the trunk the service originated on, so that trunk-specific NxDS0 services with channel-associated signaling can be emulated.
sections.plainLanguage: The voice data is cut into frames of timeslots, and the frames are packed into packets a whole number of frames at a time. A single channel is sent every 8 milliseconds, a few channels every 4, and five or more every 1 millisecond.

sections.title: How the Interworking Function Behaves
sections.content:
Edge-to-edge emulation is only possible when the two pseudowire attachment circuits are of the same type, basic NxDS0 or trunk-specific NxDS0 with channel-associated signaling, and the same bit rate; the service type and bit rate are exchanged when the pseudowire is set up. In the direction towards the packet network, the interworking function packetizes the TDM data using the configured number of payload bytes per packet, inserts sequence numbers, flags and timestamps if the RTP header is used, appends signaling sub-structures for trunk-specific services carrying the last fragment of a multiframe, prepends the CESoPSN, multiplexing layer and packet network headers, and transmits the packets.

In the direction towards the customer edge, the interworking function should include a jitter buffer, whose size should be locally configurable so that it can absorb the delay variation of the packet network. It must detect lost and misordered packets, using the sequence number in the control word or, if the RTP header is used, the RTP sequence number. Misordered packets that cannot be reordered must be discarded and treated as lost. The payload of packets marked with the L bit set should be replaced by a locally configured idle pattern even when it has not been omitted, and the function is configured to command the native service processing block to do nothing, to transmit the alarm indication pattern towards the local customer, or to send the channel idle signal on all the DS0 channels of the attachment circuit. When packets arrive with L clear and M set to 10, or with the R bit set, the same three choices apply, but using the remote alarm indication pattern instead.

Before the pseudowire is set up and after it is torn down, the function must play out the idle pattern to the TDM attachment circuit. Once the pseudowire is up, it stores received payload in the jitter buffer while still playing out the idle pattern, until a pre-configured amount of TDM data, usually half the jitter buffer, has arrived in consecutive packets, or an intermediate state timer expires. It then enters normal operation, playing out the jitter buffer contents on the required clock, performing clock recovery and optionally monitoring defects and collecting performance data. If it loses a pre-configured number of consecutive packets, or the timer expires first, it enters the packet loss state, where the idle pattern is played out and the local network-bound function marks every packet it sends with the R bit set. It leaves that state once a pre-configured number of consecutive packets have been received.

Beyond the packet loss state, the function may detect stray packets, malformed packets, an excessive packet loss rate, a buffer overrun and remote packet loss. Each defect has a state, a detection criterion that triggers the transition, and an alarm that may be reported to the management system and later cleared. Alarms are reported only when the defect persists for a pre-configured time, typically 2.5 seconds, and must be cleared after the defect has been undetected for a second pre-configured time, typically 10 seconds. Performance monitoring is optional and is performed only after the function has left its intermediate state; an error event is the insertion of a single replacement packet into the jitter buffer, an errored data block is a block played out to the attachment circuit that has seen at least one error event, and a defect is the packet loss state itself.
sections.plainLanguage: At the sending end the voice is chopped into packets; at the receiving end it is held in a buffer and played out at exactly the right rate. When packets go missing, the receiver substitutes silence or an idle pattern, tells the far end by setting a bit, and raises an alarm if the loss lasts more than about two and a half seconds.

sections.title: Quality of Service, Congestion and Security
sections.content:
If the packet network is Diffserv-enabled and provides a per-domain behavior that guarantees low jitter and low loss, the pseudowire should use that behavior under the admission and allocation rules the network has put in place. A CESoPSN pseudowire represents an inelastic, constant bit rate flow and cannot respond to congestion in a TCP-friendly manner, even though the share of bandwidth it takes stays constant, and unless precautions are taken, undiminished demand can contribute to congestion that affects network control protocols. Whenever possible the pseudowire should be carried across traffic-engineered networks offering bandwidth reservation and admission control, or forwarding prioritization and boundary traffic conditioning; IntServ domains with Guaranteed Service and Diffserv domains with Expedited Forwarding are examples. To make boundary conditioning easier over IP networks, CESoPSN packets should not use the Diffserv code point reserved for the default behavior. If the pseudowire runs over a best-effort network it should monitor packet loss to detect severe congestion, and if that is detected it should shut down in both directions for a period, as described in the PWE3 architecture. The document does not define the exact detection criteria or the shutdown method, and leaves them for further study, but notes that the performance monitoring parameters give entry and exit criteria closely correlated with the unavailability state of the emulated circuit, that the regular teardown procedures of the setup protocol should be used, and that if one end stops sending packets for long enough its peer, observing total loss, will stop sending too.

On security, CESoPSN neither enhances nor detracts from the security of the underlying packet network, and relies on it for encryption, integrity and authentication. CESoPSN pseudowires share the susceptibility of pseudowires generally to pseudowire-layer attacks, and use whatever mechanisms are developed for general pseudowires. Although a pseudowire may use an RTP header when explicit transfer of timing information is required, SRTP mechanisms cannot substitute for pseudowire-layer security. The misconnection detection capabilities of CESoPSN increase its resilience to misconfiguration and to some denial-of-service attacks, and random initialization of the sequence numbers makes known-plaintext attacks on encrypted pseudowires harder.
sections.plainLanguage: This kind of traffic cannot slow down when the network is busy, so it has to be reserved or prioritised. If the network offers only best effort, the pseudowire watches for heavy loss and, if it sees it, takes itself down in both directions rather than making things worse.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero unless indicating the start of an Associated Channel Header.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: Set when the attachment circuit has an abnormal condition.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Set by the network-bound end when the far end has lost a run of consecutive packets.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: Modifier: tells signaling packets apart and carries the remote defect indication.

fields.name: FRG
fields.desc: Fragmentation of multiframe structures; cleared except for trunk-specific services.

fields.name: LEN
fields.desc: Length of the CESoPSN packet when less than 64 bytes, otherwise zero.

fields.name: Sequence number
fields.desc: 16-bit circular counter used to detect lost packets.
